title: Improving Agents is a Data Mining Problem — Vivek Trivedy, LangChain
talk_summary: Vivek Trivedy argues that improving agents is fundamentally a data-mining loop: ship, collect traces, mine them with agents, then run data-driven experiments on prompts/harness/models. He gives concrete mechanisms for cheap trace mining, model downgrading via harness engineering, dense feedback signals, and eval generation from traces.

takeaways.what_they_do: Centralize all agent traces in one project, then send cheap agents to read other agents' traces looking for good/bad interactions, compaction degradation, and failure patterns.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we send agents to read traces from other agents... find a bunch of like good and bad interactions

takeaways.what_they_do: Start with the strongest model to prove a task is possible, then re-read those traces and engineer the harness/prompt so a cheaper open model matches the frontier trace-judging capability.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we start with Opus... once we reach that sort of like waterline, then we like look back at those traces and we see, 'Hey, can we use an open model'
takeaways.numbers: roughly matches Opus trace-judging at one to two orders of magnitude cheaper

takeaways.what_they_do: Mine trace data to auto-generate eval datasets and feedback, then hill-climb agents against those evals; treat the eval set as the definition of agent behavior.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can basically define agent behavior by showing the evals that you ran on it

takeaways.technique: Treat long traces as external queryable objects
takeaways.what_they_do: Because long coding-agent traces don't fit in a reader agent's context, store them externally and have the mining agent query into them rather than stuffing context.
Replace binary pass/fail with dense, trace-grounded feedback so the agent has a signal for what to fix next; traces are the substrate holding that feedback.
takeaways.evidence_quote: giving agents dense feedback signals... if you failed, like you wouldn't really have a good signal to figure out what you should do next

takeaways.technique: Token cost to hardware cost for high-volume inference
takeaways.what_they_do: For very high inference workloads, run a cluster for unlimited inference and spin it down when idle, converting per-token spend into hardware spend.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can move from token costs to hardware costs... for like very high inference workloads, we find it to be way cheaper just to like run a cluster
